What has changed is the ____2____ through which light reaches your eyes. The example is ordinary, but it asks us to separate an object's condition from its ____3____.

Your visual system interprets the arriving rays, and the underwater part appears in a position different from its actual one. The apparent break belongs to the ____5____, not to the straw itself. A photograph from a suitable angle can record the same ____6____.

Looking from another position changes the view. The effect therefore depends on geometry as well as the materials involved. It is not enough to say that water always makes every object look the ____7____ way. The observer's position and the direction of the light both ____8____. Keeping the glass still while moving your viewpoint can make that dependence easier to ____9____.

This does not mean vision is useless or that every appearance should be distrusted. It means appearances arise under particular ____10____. Knowing those conditions helps us interpret what we see. The straight straw is not one fact and the bent-looking image a completely unrelated ____11____. The image can be explained through the light's journey. An explanation connects observation with a ____12____ rather than merely dismissing observation as wrong.

The example also shows why a second view can be useful. It does not automatically replace the first with an equally unsupported ____13____. It offers a comparison. Together, the views help identify what remained ____14____ and what changed.
